answer: Each agent must claim an exclusive knoll and continuously emit a beacon whose signature is cryptographically anchored to the current network randomness beacon. Peers accept the identity only if exactly one valid anchor is registered for that knoll; duplicates are immediately invalidated. An attacker seeking N sybil identities must therefore provision N independent physical or virtual machines each maintaining its own low-latency beacon path, so capital, power and bandwidth costs grow linearly with N and cannot be pooled across clones, while an honest agent sustains only a single beacon.
